newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China reform may lead to Korea-style corporate giants.
newsitem.headline: China reform may lead to Korea-style corporate giants.

text.p: China's overhaul of its loss-making state enterprises could result in Chinese-style style "chaebol", or Korean conglomerates, a leading economist predicted on Friday.

The Chinese government was moving to streamline rules on bankruptcy and mergers and acquisitions to create a more efficient business environment, Deutsche Bank Group Asia-Pacific chief economist Kenneth Courtis told reporters.
"You'll end up with 25 or 30 chaebol that will cherry-pick the state companies and take the best ones," Courtis said.

Last month, Wang Zhongyu, minister of the State Economic and Trade Commission, said the government would cultivate "a batch of leader enterprises" and would encourage mergers of "inferior enterprises with superior ones".
The success of market-driven entities such as CITIC and Sinochem, which have thrived in a free market, is overshadowed by bloated enterprises created by decades of central planning.
China's state sector is estimated to employ more than 100 million workers, often in loss-making businesses.
Courtis said the government was making contingency plans for unemployment generated by state sector reforms.
"A fund has been created -- (mainland economic chief) Zhu Rongji told me this early in February -- to fund up to 10 million displaced workers over two years," Courtis said.
He said one factor driving the changes to the sector was state enterprises' high level of debt to mainland banks, with about 30 percent of mainland banks' assets now non-performing.
"That makes Thailand look in relatively good health, and Japan look downright vigorous," he said.
